Source: the BC Address Geocoder

Source: vignettes/source-bc.Rmd
source-bc.Rmd

One of this package’s seven data sources — one of the four online services. vignette("data-sources") is the overview and puts it in context.

The Province of British Columbia runs the BC Address Geocoder, a public, keyless service over the province’s own site and parcel registries. It is the highest quality address source this package can reach, and it covers one province.

bc_geocode() is the binding, "bc" is a geocode() tier, and bc_validate() re-asks it about an answer you already have.

library(cangeocode)
library(dplyr)

What this adds to the package

A second opinion from an authority, which nothing else here provides. geocode() cannot tell you whether its own answer is right — every offline tier reads NAR, so a NAR error is invisible from the inside. BC’s geocoder is a provincial address authority built on parcels and a site registry, not a compilation of what others supplied, and where it and NAR disagree BC’s answer is the more reliable of the two. That is what bc_validate() is for.

It also adds coverage, though less than the quality would suggest. As a tier it places BC addresses the offline tiers miss; but the two sources plausibly share upstream data, so it is not independent of NAR and much of what NAR is missing in BC it is missing too.

And it is the source of the only calibration the package has of what uncertainty_m = 0 is actually worth. uncertainty_m measures error this package adds relative to NAR’s point, and says nothing about NAR’s own error; BC is the one place that second quantity has been measured at all — see vignette("source-nar").

Licence

Every response carries its own copyright notice and licence link:

Copyright © 2024 Province of British Columbia

under the Open Government Licence – British Columbia. That composes with the Statistics Canada Open Licence covering NAR, so BC coordinates can be mixed into a result without further conditions — unlike the ODbL data behind osm_geocode(), which is why that one is not a tier.

Using it 

bc_geocode("525 Superior St, Victoria, BC") |>
  select(match_method, uncertainty_m, bc_score, bc_precision, bc_descriptor,
         bc_accuracy, lon, lat)
#>   match_method uncertainty_m bc_score bc_precision bc_descriptor bc_accuracy       lon     lat
#> 1     bc_civic            20      100 CIVIC_NUMBER   parcelPoint        high -123.3709 48.4177

As a tier, and as a validator:

g <- geocode(c("525 Superior St, Victoria, BC", "800 Robson St, Vancouver, BC"),
             method = c("nar", "bc"))

bc_validate(g) |>
  select(input, match_method, bc_match_method, bc_precision, bc_dist_m)
#>                           input match_method bc_match_method bc_precision    bc_dist_m
#> 1 525 Superior St, Victoria, BC nar_building        bc_civic CIVIC_NUMBER 6.864790e+00
#> 2  800 Robson St, Vancouver, BC     bc_civic        bc_civic CIVIC_NUMBER 1.253831e-09

bc_dist_m is how far BC’s answer sits from the one already obtained, and it is the column to sort on when looking for suspect rows. Note the second row: it was placed by the "bc" tier in the first place, so validating it re-asks the source that already answered and the distance is zero by construction. Validation only says something about rows an offline tier placed.

What to watch out for

The service always answers

Feed it something that does not exist and it does not fail — it returns the centre of the locality:

bc_geocode("1234 Nonexistentzzz Rd, Victoria, BC") |>
  select(match_method, bc_score, bc_precision, bc_address, bc_faults)
#>   match_method bc_score bc_precision   bc_address                           bc_faults
#> 1         none       48     LOCALITY Victoria, BC LOCALITY_INITIAL_GARBAGE notAllowed

So the presence of a result says nothing. matchPrecision is the field that decides what was actually resolved, and match_method is derived from it: bc_site and bc_civic are addresses, bc_block is interpolated along a block, and bc_street and bc_locality are answers about a place rather than an address. min_score additionally rejects matches the service itself scored poorly, and bc_faults says why it did.

Which point on the property you get — and which one you asked for

BC holds several different points for one address, and locationDescriptor selects among them. Their definitions are the service’s own:

descriptor what it is
parcelPoint a position known to be inside the parcel, usually the centroid
rooftopPoint the roof of the house or building
frontDoorPoint the front door or main entrance
accessPoint on the curb or road edge, in the middle of the driveway or access lane
routingPoint on the road centreline, directly in front of the access point
any (the default) whatever main location it holds, falling back to the access point when it holds none 
one <- "525 Superior St, Victoria, BC"

lapply(c("any", "rooftopPoint", "accessPoint", "routingPoint"), function(d) {
  bc_geocode(one, locationDescriptor = d) |>
    transmute(asked = d, bc_descriptor, bc_accuracy, lon, lat)
}) |> bind_rows()
#>          asked bc_descriptor bc_accuracy       lon      lat
#> 1          any   parcelPoint        high -123.3709 48.41770
#> 2 rooftopPoint   parcelPoint        high -123.3709 48.41770
#> 3  accessPoint   accessPoint      medium -123.3710 48.41808
#> 4 routingPoint  routingPoint      medium -123.3710 48.41811

Asking does not mean getting, which is why bc_descriptor reports what actually came back. The service does not go looking for the kind of point you named; it returns the main location it happens to hold. Over 400 NAR BC building points (data-raw/probe_bc.R), frontDoorPoint, rooftopPoint and parcelPoint each returned a point identical to any on 100% of addresses — the main location was a parcel point for 359 of the 400 and a rooftop for 19, and no request changed that. Only accessPoint and routingPoint are genuinely different points.

The default is the one closest to NAR

The NAR User Guide says a building representative point “may not correspond exactly to the physical center of the building structure itself” and may be the road access point or the driveway — which describes BC’s accessPoint almost word for word, and suggests the package should be asking for that one. Measured, it should not. Distance from NAR’s own building point, on the 378 of 400 addresses BC resolved cleanly under every descriptor:

requested p25 p50 p75 p90 within 10 m within 25 m
any / parcelPoint / frontDoorPoint / rooftopPoint 1.6 m 20.2 m 50.7 m 99.1 m 38% 57%
accessPoint 16.6 m 28.9 m 52.9 m 98.7 m 11% 43%
routingPoint 19.1 m 31.6 m 54.7 m 99.7 m 6% 36%

Paired per address, accessPoint is a median 5.3 m further from NAR than the default and routingPoint 7.7 m further. So the package’s default is already the right one, and accessPoint is what to ask for when the road-side position is what you actually want — routing, service delivery — rather than the building.

The per-address picture is more interesting than the aggregate, though. The default is the closest of the three on only 58% of addresses; accessPoint wins on 29% and routingPoint on 13%. NAR’s building points are not consistently one kind of point or the other — they are a mixture, which is exactly what the User Guide’s hedge describes. There is no single BC point that NAR is trying to be.

Note also the p25 column: the default agrees with NAR to within 1.6 m on a quarter of addresses. That is not two sources independently arriving at the same place — it is the same underlying record surfacing twice.

uncertainty_m for the bc_* tiers is not measured

It is the one set of numbers in this package that was not derived from data. BC publishes locationPositionalAccuracy as the categorical high / medium / low / coarse and no distance at all, so the metres attached to bc_site, bc_civic and the rest are the service’s precision semantics translated into deliberately pessimistic order-of-magnitude figures. Treat them as a ranking that is safe to filter on, not as an error bar comparable to the NAR tiers’.

bc_accuracy carries the categorical straight through, and it is the more honest field of the two.

It covers British Columbia only

bc_validate() skips rows outside BC rather than sending them, because the service would answer about a BC place of the same name.

Where the measurements live 

file.show(system.file("notes", "geocoding-status.md", package = "cangeocode"))

data-raw/probe_bc.R reproduces the reference-point comparison above; the geocoding status note carries the NAR-versus-BC distance distributions and what they do and do not prove.
